newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Empire strikes back, but no victory yet.
newsitem.headline: Empire strikes back, but no victory yet.

text.p: Empire East Land, beleaguered Philippine property company which has been rocked by rumours of bankruptcy, hit back on Friday by offering to buy its own shares but analysts say the benefit to its stock price may not last.
"We want to enhance shareholders value," Empire chairman Andrew Tan told reporters when asked about what prompted the buy back.
He would not give any details other than to say the purchase would be "over a period."

Empire has become the reluctant focus of investors, who have been starting to panic that the Philippines was about to follow Thailand's unhappy example of a property crash spilling over into the banking sector.
Only after repeated denials from company officials and the government officials that Empire was facing bankruptcy did the share price managed to recover from record lows earlier this week.

"Before you believe the rumours...Let Empire East give you the facts. Fact - Empire East is financially strong and stable," it said in a full-page newspaper advertisement published on the morning of its annual shareholders meeting.
Empire's share price recovered some ground on the news, rising 60 centavos ($0.02) to 5.20 pesos ($0.20), but was still below the close on Thursday.

"The company is not going bankrupt. Some of you may find it funny, but not us. The rumour has led to the loss in the value of our shares," Empire president Gerardo Garcia told shareholders at the start of their meeting on Friday.
The company has set up a damage control committee to deal with the wave of rumours about its financial health.
But analysts said any reversal in the downtrend in Empire's share price was unlikely to come soon and gains from the buy back wiould be limited.

"The negative sentiment is so strong and a buy back seems like the company is the only one supporting the issue. Quarterly results will show (if there are grounds)...for a turnaround in the share price," said Alexis Cabel, analyst at Angping & Associates Securities.
Empire's Tan said he expects profits to rise by 33 percent this year on 10 percent growth in sales.
Company earnings for the first three months are "on track," he added, but gave no details and said the figures would be out next week.
"What they are doing now is a mopping up operation. The whole sector is on a downslide and it's beyond their control," said Saturnino Mejia, research head at Guoco Securities Phils.

"A buy back is a court of last resort. Historically, it does not work in the Philippines, but I guess they have to show that something is being done. The real solution is that by the end of the year, we should see good profit results," said one broker from a foreign securities firm. Conversion $1=26.3
